newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Zajedno thinking of calling off street protests.
newsitem.headline: Zajedno thinking of calling off street protests.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders on Friday signalled a possible end of marathon street protests and a fight for the big prize by the end of the year -- presidential and parliamentary elections.

"I propose that we meet here tomorrow night and agree on our further moves," Vuk Draskovic, one of the three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, told thousands of supporters in Belgrade's central square on Friday evening.
"We cannot continue demonstrations because we believe the local councilmen will not enter the assemblies -- because they have now received their documents," he said.
The Belgrade city election commission on Thursday removed the last legal obstacle to Zajedno's assuming control over the city by verifying the mandates of the newly-elected deputies.
The Serbian parliament, at President Slobodan Milosevic's order, endorsed on Tuesday a special law reinstating Zajedno's victory in 14 towns, including Belgrade, in local elections in November.
The law was based on the findings of an OSCE mission headed by former Spanish Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez last December.
Parliament Speaker Dragan Tomic scheduled the constituent Belgrade city assembly for next Friday. The efficiency took Zajedno leaders by surprise.
"To my utter surprise, the lex specialis (special law) has so far been applied exactly according to the Gonzalez report," Draskovic said.
Zajedno leaders had promised to keep up street protests until all their city councilmen took office.
But after 87 days of massive street protests which at their peak to rallied up to 500,000 people in the biggest challenge to Milosevic's 10-year rule, Zajedno leaders now faced a stark choice.
Their dilemma was whether to continue their rallies and try toppling Milosevic -- which would be unlikely and risk the protests running out of steam and possible violent retribution by the police.
The other choice was to get off the streets, as they had promised the West, and enter a dialogue on further reforms with the ruling leftists whom they deeply distrust.
Apparently the leaders decided on the latter solution but warned they could hit the streets any time if all else fails.
"We should not waste time but decide on our strategic objective -- how to eliminate this regime," Draskovic said.
"We have achieved an enormous victory -- this is the first time since 1944, when they (the Communists) marched into this city, that they have accepted a single demand of the people.

But in a possible setback, independent Belgrade news agency Beta reported the city election commission in Sabac refused to reinstate Zajedno's majority of 38 seats in the local 69-seat assembly saying the "special law was not binding". The report could not be immediately confirmed.

Zajedno leaders have made clear that with their victories reinstated they were setting their sights on higher targets, including reforms and free access to the state-run media which helps to keep Milosevic in power.
"It will need a lot of work, we must draft plans and platforms, deblock the media -- but we cannot achieve it if you say: all or nothing," Zajedno leader Vesna Pesic said.
"We should not exhaust ourselves and then just die off. Let us distribute our forces so we can score the big goal at the end of the year," she said referring to the Serbian elections.

Serbia's ruling leftists and state media on Friday issued warnings against street protests which the Belgrade students ignored, attempting to march past Milosevic's home and being politely but resolutely turned back by police.
The Yugoslav United Left (JUL), headed by Milosevic's powerful wife Mirjana Markovic warned Zajedno leaders against "terrorising" citizens.
State Radio Belgrade on Friday commented on the protests through streets in which members of the ruling elite live.
The marches recalled the "dark times from our past, when houses of patriots, liberators and especially Jews were marked in a sign of retaliation or destruction," it said.
